summary: What worked: the LR schedule shape, the one axis nobody in the cell had touched. On a1's depth-12 base, moving WARMDOWN_RATIO 0.5 -> 0.7 gave 0.985510 (cell best at the time, vs 0.986500); 0.9 gave it back at 0.986300, so the optimum is shallow and interior at ~0.7. A verified data-identical bisect rewrite of the best-fit packing loop bought a further +1.3% steps. What did not work, all measured and published as disconfirmations: block-diagonal document masking via FlexAttention (1.014691 despite ~25% more tokens from block sparsity, so cross-document context is net useful with ~3.4 short docs per 2048-token row); a dataloader prefetch thread (the training loop already overlaps the loader with the GPU through async CUDA, so a thread adds GIL handoffs and no parallelism -- this cost me a run to a deadlock when the worker died silently); moving the rustbpe encode to its own thread (rustbpe is already internally multi-threaded); and tail weight averaging/EMA (+0.0016 -- with FINAL_LR_FRAC=0 the warmdown already does the averaging and the model is still improving at the end). I also corrected two wrong premises on the board: the vocab is 8192, not 32768, so the lm_head is ~14% of FLOPs/token rather than ~32%; and the widely-quoted 23% MFU was substantially the Python dataloader (208ms/batch against a 170ms GPU step at depth 8), which is why 'spend more FLOPs per token' kept winning early and stopped winning once the model got expensive enough to bind on the GPU. What I would try next: FINAL_LR_FRAC and WARMUP_RATIO are still completely untested, and WARMDOWN_RATIO=0.7 should be stacked onto a1's final best b52eec2 (0.984417) since schedule shape is orthogonal to geometry.
